doc_screened_files.reason: This is the direct panic site: the ICE is raised by `invalid_hir_id_for_typeck_results` in this file when a `HirId` from the thread_local macro closure is inserted under the wrong `hir_owner`. The failure message and query stack point here first.

This file builds the per-owner HIR node index and parent map, so any misassigned `HirId`/owner relationship for the closure inside the const generic would originate here. The bug looks like a broken ownership invariant that this pass is responsible for maintaining.

It coordinates lowering of item owners, generics, and owner bookkeeping into HIR. The failing code is inside an impl-level const generic, which makes this file a strong upstream suspect for creating the wrong owner context.

The observed bad node is a closure expression (`|init|`) produced inside the macro expansion. Closure lowering happens here, so an incorrect body owner or nested-expression ownership boundary could explain why the closure ends up in the impl's `TypeckResults`.

The ICE happens during `thir_body` construction, and this file owns the THIR-building driver for a body. If THIR is queried for a node from the wrong owner, this is one of the first downstream places that would expose it.

The problematic node is an expression and closure, and this file lowers expressions into THIR. It is a plausible place for the closure body to be attached to the wrong HIR owner during THIR construction.

This file synthesizes generics for special forms such as closures, const blocks, and anonymous consts. Because the crash involves a const generic context and nested closure, incorrect generic/owner synthesis here could feed the later typeck mismatch.

The failing code originates from `thread_local!`, a macro expansion path. This module performs macro-by-example transcription, so it is a credible place for generated closure spans or node ownership to be attached incorrectly before lowering.

Anonymous consts and const arguments get their types through this collection path. Since the reproducer places a macro invocation inside a const generic, this file is a plausible intermediate source of the mismatched body/typeck ownership.

The reproducer combines an impl, a const generic, and macro-generated nested bodies, all of which depend on correct binder and owner resolution. This file is a lower-priority but still relevant suspect for misclassifying nested bound vars or opaque/macro-generated scopes.
